gv-cv-bubble-wide: every bubble reads level — and no two are parallel
gv-cv-amber-wide: amber dashed: disc of finite radius, computed
gv-cv-dist-from-centre: distance from the centre of the map (km)
gv-cv-flat-wide: infinite plane: no change with height, ever
gv-cv-any-flat-wide: any flat model: one value everywhere
td-c1: Neither body is held up: each falls towards the other and misses, once a month around their common centre. The whole Earth falls towards the Moon with the pull its centre feels.
td-c2a: Near side +{n} %, far side −{f} % compared with the centre: the pull weakens with distance.
td-c2b: Take away what the centre feels (the whole Earth falls with it): the rest stretches the Earth along the line to the Moon and squeezes it across. Two bulges, not one.
td-c3: The bulges stay lined up with the Moon while the Earth turns under them: every port passes under one bulge, then the other. High water every 12 h 25 min, 50 minutes later each day, as the Moon rises 50 minutes later.
td-c4: Kepler III, GM/d³ = (2π/T)², gives the Sun's pull against the Moon's from the month, the year and the masses: (27.32/365.26)² × (1 + 81.3) = {r}. Aligned at new and full moon: spring tides; at right angles: neap tides, every 14.77 days.
td-c5: Tilted bulges: the port passes through the thick part of one and the edge of the other. One high is bigger than the other each day; where the sea damps the 12-hour wave, only the daily one is left, as at Pensacola.
td-c6: Water climbs towards a pull. On a plane every point is on the same side of the Moon, so there is one hump, under it, and one high water a day. The far-side bulge needs a body that falls towards the Moon as a whole: a globe.
td-t1: 1. The Earth and the Moon fall around each other
td-t2: 2. The Moon pulls the near side harder than the far side
td-t3: 3. Two bulges, and the Earth turns under them
td-t4: 4. The Sun adds a smaller pair: spring and neap tides
td-t5: 5. The Moon off the equator: the two tides of a day differ
td-t6: 6. The flat model's best case: a nearby Moon over a plane
td-bary: + barycentre: 4,670 km from the Earth's centre, inside the Earth
td-st2a: black: the Moon's pull, all to one scale
td-st2b: blue: pull minus the centre's, drawn 20× longer
td-s3: height at the port, two lunar days (24 h 50 min each)
td-s4: height at the port over one month (29.5 days)
td-s5: height at 45° N, two lunar days
td-st6: shading: water level, any scale; same for any height or mass of the Moon
td-s6: height at the port, two lunar days
td-fx-alt: The Earth with the Moon far to the right. Black arrows: the Moon's pull at the near side, the centre and the far side, slightly longer at the near side. Blue arrows: each minus the centre's pull: outward at the near and far sides, inward at the top and bottom
td-fxk-alt: Left: the Moon goes round the Earth in 27.32 days; right: the Earth goes round the Sun in 365.26 days. For each, GM over d cubed equals two pi over the period, squared, so the strength of each tide follows from its period, with the Moon's share of the Earth–Moon pair, 1 part in 82.3
td-spec-alt: Amplitude against frequency for one year of hourly sea level at five tide gauges. Every record has lines at the frequencies the Moon and Sun set, marked O1, K1, N2, M2, S2: Brest's M2 line is 2 metres high, Pensacola's diurnal lines dominate
td-spec-x: cycles per day (each row to its own height)
td-mon-alt: Sea level through March 2018 at Brest and at Pensacola. Brest's range swells at new and full moon and shrinks at the quarters; Pensacola has one tide a day, largest when the Moon is farthest from the equator and almost none when it crosses it
ss-alt: Twice-daily tide (M2 amplitude) measured at the gauges of six seas, on a logarithmic scale: about 1.3 m on the Atlantic coast of Europe and 3.3 m in the Bay of Fundy, 6 cm in the Gulf of Mexico, 7 cm in the Mediterranean, 2 cm in the Black Sea, under 1 cm in the Baltic. Open circles: the largest tide a closed basin of that length could have from the pull alone; Lake Superior and Lake Geneva added
ss-key: bar: middle half of the gauges · dot: median · ring: closed-basin bound A·L/R
ss-bay-alt: A bay of length L and depth h open to the ocean at one end. The tide entering from the ocean reflects at the closed end; if the time for the wave to go in and out twice, 4L over the square root of g h, is close to 12 hours 25 minutes, each tide adds to the last and the range at the head of the bay grows
ss-bay-s: a bay open at one end
tg-c1: The surface the pull would give the water (shading, and the outline drawn out into two bulges) turns with the Moon; each spike is one tide gauge, its tide at that instant from its own measured constants. Same clock everywhere, but each coast is early or late: the spikes do not ride the bulges.
tg-c2: The Moon's twice-daily line alone. The real M2 wave runs round each ocean basin, and has points where it vanishes (spikes that never grow): the sea answers the pull with its own delays.
tg-c3: One picture per lunar day: the Earth is back in the same place under the Moon, so the twice-daily tide is frozen. What still changes is the Sun's share: spikes swell at new and full moon, shrink at the quarters.
tg-t1: 1. The pull of the Moon and the Sun, and the tide at {n} gauges
tg-t2: 2. The Moon's twice-daily line, M2, alone
tg-t3: 3. One month, seen once every lunar day
tg-st: heights drawn {f} times higher, the same for the surface and the spikes
tg-l-eq: sea shaded by the equilibrium height
tg-l-cut: ring: tide larger than drawn (spike cut at {m} m)
